name: Circuit Breaker
intent: Stop calling a dependency that is failing, fail fast instead, and check now and then whether it has recovered.
scenario: The checkout service calls a payment provider. The provider starts timing out. Each checkout now waits 30 seconds before failing, threads pile up, and soon the whole shop is down even though only payments were broken.
problem: Calling a failing service is slow (timeouts) and makes things worse: callers hold threads and connections while they wait, and the struggling service gets more traffic exactly when it needs a break. One broken dependency becomes a cascading failure across the system.

howItWorks.title: Closed: calls go through, failures are counted
howItWorks.text: In normal operation the breaker is closed. Every call passes through and the breaker watches the results, usually the number of failures in a row or the failure percentage over a recent window.

howItWorks.title: Open: trip when failures cross the threshold
howItWorks.text: When failures pass the threshold, the breaker opens. Calls now fail immediately without touching the dependency, which frees the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover.

howItWorks.title: Fail fast, and fall back if possible
howItWorks.text: While open, the caller gets an instant error and can use a fallback: a cached value, a default, a queue for later, or a clear message. A fast, honest failure beats a slow one.

howItWorks.title: Half-open: let one probe through after a cool-down
howItWorks.text: After a timeout the breaker moves to half-open and allows a small number of trial calls. If they succeed it closes again. If one fails it re-opens and the timer restarts.

howItWorks.title: Tune it to the dependency
howItWorks.text: The threshold, the window and the cool-down should match real behaviour. Too sensitive and it trips on noise; too relaxed and it trips after the damage is done. Expose its state in metrics and alert when it opens.

pros: Failures become fast instead of slow, which protects threads and connections
Stops piling load on a dependency that is already struggling
Prevents one failing service from cascading through the system
cons: Needs sensible thresholds; wrong values cause false trips or late trips
Callers need a fallback or a good error, which takes design work
Can hide a problem if nobody watches the breaker state
Adds state to track, and with many instances each keeps its own view
whenToUse: Calls to remote services that can be slow or down
Dependencies where a fallback or a degraded answer is acceptable
Any call chain where a slow dependency could exhaust your threads
whenNotToUse: Calls inside one process that cannot fail independently
Operations that must always be attempted and have no useful fallback or error path
As a substitute for timeouts: you need both
pitfalls: No timeout on the call itself, so the breaker never sees a failure until much too late
Counting client errors (400s) as failures, which trips the breaker for bad input
Letting a flood of requests through in half-open instead of a single probe
Silent fallbacks that hide an outage for hours
